summary: Flame in Freefall predicts how spacecraft cabin materials burn in microgravity at the oxygen levels planned for lunar habitats, and recommends which fire experiment NASA should run next. NASA's microgravity data for solid materials (BASS-II, ISS) stops at 22% oxygen, while proposed lunar habitat atmospheres use 26.5% to 34%. We hand-transcribed 123 BASS-II tests into 430 data points and trained a model that gives the probability a flame survives for five cabin materials, at any oxygen level and airflow, with a 90% uncertainty range. A test-selection method then picks the most informative next experiment. Replaying NASA's own BASS-II rod campaign, it learned the fire limit with 14% fewer tests than the order NASA ran them in, and 27% fewer than spreading tests evenly. Our predictions for the recommended tests are frozen and published with SHA-256 checksums, so NASA can score them when the tests are run.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Flame in Freefall is a web dashboard and analysis pipeline built on NASA's BASS-II microgravity combustion data. It answers three questions: will a given cabin material keep burning at a given oxygen level and airflow in microgravity; which experiment should be run next to learn the most; and how confident is each answer.

HOW IT WORKS

BASS-II records test outcomes only as free-text notes, so we transcribed 123 tests into 430 data points, keeping NASA's original text beside every point. Airflow logged as fan settings was converted with NASA's own fan calibration data. 278 points (15 extinctions, five materials) were usable; the rest are kept and flagged with the reason.

A weighted logistic regression on oxygen, airflow and material gives the probability that a flame survives. 100 bootstrap models give a 90% range for every prediction. Validated by hiding one whole test at a time, the model reached a balanced accuracy of 0.80 against 0.76 for a fitted oxygen-threshold rule.

The next-experiment method has three tracks: Refine (where the models disagree most, inside a trust region), Explore (a controlled 3-point oxygen step towards lunar air) and Bracket (finding the limit for materials that never went out). Replaying NASA's BASS-II rod campaign test by test, our method reached the final model's accuracy in 11.2 tests on average, against 13 for NASA's original order, 15.4 for evenly spread tests, 17.9 for random order and 23.1 for testing the highest oxygen first.

RESULTS

At 5 cm/s airflow and ISS pressure, PMMA rods in concurrent flow extinguish below about 15.9% oxygen, and PMMA rods in opposed flow and thin PMMA film below about 17.5%. All are predicted to burn at both lunar set-points (an extrapolation, labelled as such). SIBAL fabric and thick PMMA never extinguished in any BASS-II test, so their limits are still unknown; our Bracket tests target them.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

Our predictions for the recommended tests were frozen before anyone runs them and published with SHA-256 checksums in a public GitHub commit, so NASA can score them independently. The test-selection method was validated on NASA's own campaign, not on simulated data.

BENEFITS AND FACTORS CONSIDERED

Cost: each ISS combustion test uses scarce crew time and hardware; fewer tests to reach the same answer saves both. Accessibility: the dashboard is free, needs no install or login, and all code and data are open on GitHub. Safety: every prediction shows how far it is from tested conditions. Users can also enter new results and retrain the model.

LIMITATIONS

All BASS-II data is at ISS cabin pressure (14.7 psia); reduced habitat pressure is not in the data. Predictions above 22.2% oxygen are extrapolations. The replay covers PMMA rod tests only.

TOOLS

Python, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn, matplotlib, Plotly, Streamlit Community Cloud, Google Colab, GitHub.

Code and data: https://github.com/hunter-vz/flame-in-freefall

If the dashboard is asleep, click "Yes, get this app back up"; it loads in under a minute.
